properties.name: Greptime | The Single Database for Observability on S3
properties.description:
GreptimeDB is the open-source Observability 2.0 database — treating metrics, logs, and traces as unified wide events instead of three separate pillars.

The three-pillar model (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger) creates data silos, redundant infrastructure, and cross-system correlation pain. GreptimeDB replaces all three with one columnar engine on object storage, enabling cross-signal SQL JOINs, up to 50x cost reduction, and native support for emerging workloads like AI agent observability.

Why teams switch:
▪️Logs: Full-text indexing where Loki only indexes labels. 10x faster queries, 30% lower TCO. (OB Cloud: billions of logs daily across 170+ availability zones.)
▪️Metrics: Compute-storage separation — no more Thanos/Mimir complexity. SQL + PromQL replaces Prometheus + your data warehouse.
▪️Traces: Columnar storage vs. ES inverted indexes — 45x less storage, Jaeger-compatible, one-week migration.
▪️AI/LLM: Store high-volume conversation data, agent traces, and token metrics via OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions.

Written in Rust, OpenTelemetry-native, deploys on Kubernetes with compute-storage separation. Used in production by teams processing billions of data points daily.

▪️Open-source: https://github.com/GreptimeTeam/greptimedb
▪️Learn more in Why GreptimeDB: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/why-greptimedb/
▪️Learn about Observability 2.0: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/observability-2/
▪️Enterprise & Cloud: https://greptime.com

# Manifest

Manifest is a Technology, Information and Internet company. ManifestIT is a change observability platform that helps intelligently evaluate risk, quantify impact, and break down silos between tools and teams. Manifest employs 24 people. ## About

Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has l

properties.name: Manifest
properties.description:
Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has lived in the heads of senior engineers, architects, and platform teams. A developer who needs it pings someone, digs through Slack, or learns it the hard way after an outage. That works, slowly. Agents don't have that option at all. Connection pool limits, IAM scopes, mesh policies, secret bindings, downstream consumers, live drift—none of it is in the code, and none of it is in any place an agent can reach.

We've built Manifest to compile that context into software. We continuously assemble a deterministic, time-versioned graph of the customer's full application stack: code, IaC, cloud, Kubernetes, IAM, secrets, mesh, CI/CD, on-prem. The architectural commitment is retrieval separated from reasoning. The graph is built once, continuously, and queryable as data, so the agents reasoning on top don't each have to investigate the environment from scratch. The graph is the context layer that developers and coding agents query before they make a change, so the code (whether written by a human or an agent) fits the system it's about to touch. Because the graph captures every change attributed to actor and timestamp, configuration drift and unauthorized changes surface the moment they happen instead of being discovered weeks later in an outage or audit.

Manifest works from the earliest moments of the lifecycle. Developers and agents query the graph in dev to understand blast radius before code is written. CI pipelines query it to validate changes before merge. Staging queries it to catch drift between IaC and actual state. By the time a change reaches production, it's already been validated at every step. One graph, every agent.

properties.name: Core0
properties.description:
AI systems fail differently from traditional software. A rogue agent makes an innocent-looking database query that chokes the DB, congests the network, and triggers a cascade of downstream failures — none of which appear in the agent's own logs. Meanwhile, your telemetry bill keeps climbing while your team still can't find root cause fast enough.
FFWD is the AI infrastructure intelligence platform any AI app — Claude, Copilot, Codex, or your own autonomous infrastructure agent — can consume through MCP. We don't ship another agent for you to adopt. We give the AI app you already use the AI infrastructure depth no one else delivers: silicon-to-semantic telemetry, cross-domain anomaly correlation, and execution risk scoring before agents act on production.
Four interlocking capabilities on one stack:
High-performance telemetry pipeline — ingest, filter, enrich, and route millions of events per second, multi TB per day. FFWD is built in Rust. No vendor lock-in.
Full-stack anomaly detection — our Signal Correlation Model applies eight distinct ML model categories across logs, metrics, traces, GPU telemetry, and container events. No rules to write. No topology map required. Operational from day one.
Cross-domain correlation — when anomalies appear in unrelated systems at the same time, FFWD's marker correlation engine finds the statistical link. Root cause hidden in a GPU thermal trend, a sequence anomaly in a Python service, and a network rate spike? FFWD connects them.
Agent Assurance — a pre-task execution risk score before infrastructure agents act, and a confidence score after. A quantitative Go/No-Go gate grounded in live full-stack anomaly intelligence, not static rules.
These aren't four products. The pipeline feeds the anomaly model. The anomaly model powers the risk score. The risk score is only trustworthy because the data underneath it is complete.
Built for engineering teams running AI agents on production infrastructure.

entity.name: Greptime | The Single Database for Observability on S3
entity.description:
GreptimeDB is the open-source Observability 2.0 database — treating metrics, logs, and traces as unified wide events instead of three separate pillars.

The three-pillar model (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger) creates data silos, redundant infrastructure, and cross-system correlation pain. GreptimeDB replaces all three with one columnar engine on object storage, enabling cross-signal SQL JOINs, up to 50x cost reduction, and native support for emerging workloads like AI agent observability.

Why teams switch:
▪️Logs: Full-text indexing where Loki only indexes labels. 10x faster queries, 30% lower TCO. (OB Cloud: billions of logs daily across 170+ availability zones.)
▪️Metrics: Compute-storage separation — no more Thanos/Mimir complexity. SQL + PromQL replaces Prometheus + your data warehouse.
▪️Traces: Columnar storage vs. ES inverted indexes — 45x less storage, Jaeger-compatible, one-week migration.
▪️AI/LLM: Store high-volume conversation data, agent traces, and token metrics via OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions.

Written in Rust, OpenTelemetry-native, deploys on Kubernetes with compute-storage separation. Used in production by teams processing billions of data points daily.

▪️Open-source: https://github.com/GreptimeTeam/greptimedb
▪️Learn more in Why GreptimeDB: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/why-greptimedb/
▪️Learn about Observability 2.0: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/observability-2/
▪️Enterprise & Cloud: https://greptime.com

entity.name: Manifest
entity.description:
Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has lived in the heads of senior engineers, architects, and platform teams. A developer who needs it pings someone, digs through Slack, or learns it the hard way after an outage. That works, slowly. Agents don't have that option at all. Connection pool limits, IAM scopes, mesh policies, secret bindings, downstream consumers, live drift—none of it is in the code, and none of it is in any place an agent can reach.

We've built Manifest to compile that context into software. We continuously assemble a deterministic, time-versioned graph of the customer's full application stack: code, IaC, cloud, Kubernetes, IAM, secrets, mesh, CI/CD, on-prem. The architectural commitment is retrieval separated from reasoning. The graph is built once, continuously, and queryable as data, so the agents reasoning on top don't each have to investigate the environment from scratch. The graph is the context layer that developers and coding agents query before they make a change, so the code (whether written by a human or an agent) fits the system it's about to touch. Because the graph captures every change attributed to actor and timestamp, configuration drift and unauthorized changes surface the moment they happen instead of being discovered weeks later in an outage or audit.

Manifest works from the earliest moments of the lifecycle. Developers and agents query the graph in dev to understand blast radius before code is written. CI pipelines query it to validate changes before merge. Staging queries it to catch drift between IaC and actual state. By the time a change reaches production, it's already been validated at every step. One graph, every agent.

High-performance telemetry pipeline — ingest, filter, enrich, and route millions of events per second, multi TB per day. FFWD is built in Rust. No vendor lock-in.

Agent Assurance — a pre-task execution risk score before infrastructure agents act, and a confidence score after. A quantitative Go/No-Go gate grounded in live full-stack anomaly intelligence, not static rules.
These aren't four products. The pipeline feeds the anomaly model. The anomaly model powers the risk score. The risk score is only trustworthy because the data underneath it is complete.
Built for engineering teams running AI agents on production infrastructure.

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B sales benchmark.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company — the company a sales operator is targeting.
  • A CANDIDATE company — a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide whether the CANDIDATE is a plausible lookalike of the SEED for
B2B sales prospecting. A plausible lookalike is a company a sales rep
working the SEED account would also want to work — same kind of
business model, overlapping product category, or buyer persona.

Rules:
  - relevant = true only when the candidate is clearly the same kind of
    company (same model + overlapping customer or buyer persona).
  - Require both: (1) the candidate's primary product/service overlaps a core
    offering of the seed, and (2) the same buyer or user would reasonably
    evaluate both for the same job to be done. A shared generic taxonomy label
    or keyword is not enough.
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. Those are not benchmark
    constraints: a smaller or larger company can be a relevant lookalike.
    Ignore any such metadata in the candidate record when deciding relevance.
  - relevant = false for unrelated industries, parent companies,
    customers/clients of the seed, agencies/consultancies that serve the
    category (rather than competing), and parody/duplicate entries.
  - When in doubt, label false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words.

Examples:
  - HubSpot ↔ a smaller CRM/marketing-automation platform: true.
  - HubSpot ↔ a lead-generation agency using HubSpot for clients: false.
  - Shopify ↔ an online-store/e-commerce platform: true.
  - Shopify ↔ a payment processor with no storefront platform: false.
  - Grab ↔ a ride-hailing marketplace: true.
  - Grab ↔ a traditional car-rental operator with no on-demand marketplace: false.
  - Rippling ↔ a smaller HRIS/payroll platform: true.
  - Rippling ↔ device-security software for mobile workers: false.
  - Brex ↔ a corporate-card and spend-management platform: true.
  - Brex ↔ consumer personal-finance budgeting software: false.
  - OpenAI ↔ a foundation-model/API company: true.
  - OpenAI ↔ a consultancy that implements AI tools for clients: false.
  - Datadog ↔ an application-performance-monitoring and observability platform: true.
  - Datadog ↔ a generic IT consulting firm: false.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ an endpoint-security platform: true.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ a general-purpose IT monitoring tool with no security product: false.
  - Procore ↔ construction project-management software: true.
  - Procore ↔ a construction contractor: false.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ field-service management software for trades businesses: true.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ a plumbing company that uses field-service software: false.
  - Teladoc ↔ a virtual-care/telehealth platform: true.
  - Teladoc ↔ a health-insurance carrier with no telehealth product: false.
  - Veeva ↔ life-sciences CRM or clinical-operations software: true.
  - Veeva ↔ a generic CRM with no life-sciences focus: false.

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B sales benchmark.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company — the company a sales operator is targeting.
  • A CANDIDATE company — a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide whether the CANDIDATE is a plausible lookalike of the SEED for
B2B sales prospecting. A plausible lookalike is a company a sales rep
working the SEED account would also want to work — same kind of
business model, overlapping product category, or buyer persona.

Rules:
  - relevant = true only when the candidate is clearly the same kind of
    company (same model + overlapping customer or buyer persona).
  - Require both: (1) the candidate's primary product/service overlaps a core
    offering of the seed, and (2) the same buyer or user would reasonably
    evaluate both for the same job to be done. A shared generic taxonomy label
    or keyword is not enough.
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. Those are not benchmark
    constraints: a smaller or larger company can be a relevant lookalike.
    Ignore any such metadata in the candidate record when deciding relevance.
  - relevant = false for unrelated industries, parent companies,
    customers/clients of the seed, agencies/consultancies that serve the
    category (rather than competing), and parody/duplicate entries.
  - When in doubt, label false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words.

Examples:
  - HubSpot ↔ a smaller CRM/marketing-automation platform: true.
  - HubSpot ↔ a lead-generation agency using HubSpot for clients: false.
  - Shopify ↔ an online-store/e-commerce platform: true.
  - Shopify ↔ a payment processor with no storefront platform: false.
  - Grab ↔ a ride-hailing marketplace: true.
  - Grab ↔ a traditional car-rental operator with no on-demand marketplace: false.
  - Rippling ↔ a smaller HRIS/payroll platform: true.
  - Rippling ↔ device-security software for mobile workers: false.
  - Brex ↔ a corporate-card and spend-management platform: true.
  - Brex ↔ consumer personal-finance budgeting software: false.
  - OpenAI ↔ a foundation-model/API company: true.
  - OpenAI ↔ a consultancy that implements AI tools for clients: false.
  - Datadog ↔ an application-performance-monitoring and observability platform: true.
  - Datadog ↔ a generic IT consulting firm: false.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ an endpoint-security platform: true.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ a general-purpose IT monitoring tool with no security product: false.
  - Procore ↔ construction project-management software: true.
  - Procore ↔ a construction contractor: false.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ field-service management software for trades businesses: true.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ a plumbing company that uses field-service software: false.
  - Teladoc ↔ a virtual-care/telehealth platform: true.
  - Teladoc ↔ a health-insurance carrier with no telehealth product: false.
  - Veeva ↔ life-sciences CRM or clinical-operations software: true.
  - Veeva ↔ a generic CRM with no life-sciences focus: false.

properties.name: Greptime | The Single Database for Observability on S3
properties.description:
GreptimeDB is the open-source Observability 2.0 database — treating metrics, logs, and traces as unified wide events instead of three separate pillars.

The three-pillar model (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger) creates data silos, redundant infrastructure, and cross-system correlation pain. GreptimeDB replaces all three with one columnar engine on object storage, enabling cross-signal SQL JOINs, up to 50x cost reduction, and native support for emerging workloads like AI agent observability.

Why teams switch:
▪️Logs: Full-text indexing where Loki only indexes labels. 10x faster queries, 30% lower TCO. (OB Cloud: billions of logs daily across 170+ availability zones.)
▪️Metrics: Compute-storage separation — no more Thanos/Mimir complexity. SQL + PromQL replaces Prometheus + your data warehouse.
▪️Traces: Columnar storage vs. ES inverted indexes — 45x less storage, Jaeger-compatible, one-week migration.
▪️AI/LLM: Store high-volume conversation data, agent traces, and token metrics via OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions.

Written in Rust, OpenTelemetry-native, deploys on Kubernetes with compute-storage separation. Used in production by teams processing billions of data points daily.

▪️Open-source: https://github.com/GreptimeTeam/greptimedb
▪️Learn more in Why GreptimeDB: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/why-greptimedb/
▪️Learn about Observability 2.0: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/observability-2/
▪️Enterprise & Cloud: https://greptime.com

properties.name: Core0
properties.description:
AI systems fail differently from traditional software. A rogue agent makes an innocent-looking database query that chokes the DB, congests the network, and triggers a cascade of downstream failures — none of which appear in the agent's own logs. Meanwhile, your telemetry bill keeps climbing while your team still can't find root cause fast enough.
FFWD is the AI infrastructure intelligence platform any AI app — Claude, Copilot, Codex, or your own autonomous infrastructure agent — can consume through MCP. We don't ship another agent for you to adopt. We give the AI app you already use the AI infrastructure depth no one else delivers: silicon-to-semantic telemetry, cross-domain anomaly correlation, and execution risk scoring before agents act on production.
Four interlocking capabilities on one stack:
High-performance telemetry pipeline — ingest, filter, enrich, and route millions of events per second, multi TB per day. FFWD is built in Rust. No vendor lock-in.
Full-stack anomaly detection — our Signal Correlation Model applies eight distinct ML model categories across logs, metrics, traces, GPU telemetry, and container events. No rules to write. No topology map required. Operational from day one.
Cross-domain correlation — when anomalies appear in unrelated systems at the same time, FFWD's marker correlation engine finds the statistical link. Root cause hidden in a GPU thermal trend, a sequence anomaly in a Python service, and a network rate spike? FFWD connects them.
Agent Assurance — a pre-task execution risk score before infrastructure agents act, and a confidence score after. A quantitative Go/No-Go gate grounded in live full-stack anomaly intelligence, not static rules.
These aren't four products. The pipeline feeds the anomaly model. The anomaly model powers the risk score. The risk score is only trustworthy because the data underneath it is complete.
Built for engineering teams running AI agents on production infrastructure.

## About

Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has l

properties.name: Manifest
properties.description:
Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has lived in the heads of senior engineers, architects, and platform teams. A developer who needs it pings someone, digs through Slack, or learns it the hard way after an outage. That works, slowly. Agents don't have that option at all. Connection pool limits, IAM scopes, mesh policies, secret bindings, downstream consumers, live drift—none of it is in the code, and none of it is in any place an agent can reach.

We've built Manifest to compile that context into software. We continuously assemble a deterministic, time-versioned graph of the customer's full application stack: code, IaC, cloud, Kubernetes, IAM, secrets, mesh, CI/CD, on-prem. The architectural commitment is retrieval separated from reasoning. The graph is built once, continuously, and queryable as data, so the agents reasoning on top don't each have to investigate the environment from scratch. The graph is the context layer that developers and coding agents query before they make a change, so the code (whether written by a human or an agent) fits the system it's about to touch. Because the graph captures every change attributed to actor and timestamp, configuration drift and unauthorized changes surface the moment they happen instead of being discovered weeks later in an outage or audit.

Manifest works from the earliest moments of the lifecycle. Developers and agents query the graph in dev to understand blast radius before code is written. CI pipelines query it to validate changes before merge. Staging queries it to catch drift between IaC and actual state. By the time a change reaches production, it's already been validated at every step. One graph, every agent.

entity.name: Greptime | The Single Database for Observability on S3
entity.description:
GreptimeDB is the open-source Observability 2.0 database — treating metrics, logs, and traces as unified wide events instead of three separate pillars.

The three-pillar model (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger) creates data silos, redundant infrastructure, and cross-system correlation pain. GreptimeDB replaces all three with one columnar engine on object storage, enabling cross-signal SQL JOINs, up to 50x cost reduction, and native support for emerging workloads like AI agent observability.

Why teams switch:
▪️Logs: Full-text indexing where Loki only indexes labels. 10x faster queries, 30% lower TCO. (OB Cloud: billions of logs daily across 170+ availability zones.)
▪️Metrics: Compute-storage separation — no more Thanos/Mimir complexity. SQL + PromQL replaces Prometheus + your data warehouse.
▪️Traces: Columnar storage vs. ES inverted indexes — 45x less storage, Jaeger-compatible, one-week migration.
▪️AI/LLM: Store high-volume conversation data, agent traces, and token metrics via OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions.

Written in Rust, OpenTelemetry-native, deploys on Kubernetes with compute-storage separation. Used in production by teams processing billions of data points daily.

▪️Open-source: https://github.com/GreptimeTeam/greptimedb
▪️Learn more in Why GreptimeDB: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/why-greptimedb/
▪️Learn about Observability 2.0: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/observability-2/
▪️Enterprise & Cloud: https://greptime.com

entity.name: Core0
entity.description:
AI systems fail differently from traditional software. A rogue agent makes an innocent-looking database query that chokes the DB, congests the network, and triggers a cascade of downstream failures — none of which appear in the agent's own logs. Meanwhile, your telemetry bill keeps climbing while your team still can't find root cause fast enough.
FFWD is the AI infrastructure intelligence platform any AI app — Claude, Copilot, Codex, or your own autonomous infrastructure agent — can consume through MCP. We don't ship another agent for you to adopt. We give the AI app you already use the AI infrastructure depth no one else delivers: silicon-to-semantic telemetry, cross-domain anomaly correlation, and execution risk scoring before agents act on production.
Four interlocking capabilities on one stack:
High-performance telemetry pipeline — ingest, filter, enrich, and route millions of events per second, multi TB per day. FFWD is built in Rust. No vendor lock-in.
Full-stack anomaly detection — our Signal Correlation Model applies eight distinct ML model categories across logs, metrics, traces, GPU telemetry, and container events. No rules to write. No topology map required. Operational from day one.
Cross-domain correlation — when anomalies appear in unrelated systems at the same time, FFWD's marker correlation engine finds the statistical link. Root cause hidden in a GPU thermal trend, a sequence anomaly in a Python service, and a network rate spike? FFWD connects them.
Agent Assurance — a pre-task execution risk score before infrastructure agents act, and a confidence score after. A quantitative Go/No-Go gate grounded in live full-stack anomaly intelligence, not static rules.
These aren't four products. The pipeline feeds the anomaly model. The anomaly model powers the risk score. The risk score is only trustworthy because the data underneath it is complete.
Built for engineering teams running AI agents on production infrastructure.

entity.name: Manifest
entity.description:
Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has lived in the heads of senior engineers, architects, and platform teams. A developer who needs it pings someone, digs through Slack, or learns it the hard way after an outage. That works, slowly. Agents don't have that option at all. Connection pool limits, IAM scopes, mesh policies, secret bindings, downstream consumers, live drift—none of it is in the code, and none of it is in any place an agent can reach.

We've built Manifest to compile that context into software. We continuously assemble a deterministic, time-versioned graph of the customer's full application stack: code, IaC, cloud, Kubernetes, IAM, secrets, mesh, CI/CD, on-prem. The architectural commitment is retrieval separated from reasoning. The graph is built once, continuously, and queryable as data, so the agents reasoning on top don't each have to investigate the environment from scratch. The graph is the context layer that developers and coding agents query before they make a change, so the code (whether written by a human or an agent) fits the system it's about to touch. Because the graph captures every change attributed to actor and timestamp, configuration drift and unauthorized changes surface the moment they happen instead of being discovered weeks later in an outage or audit.

Manifest works from the earliest moments of the lifecycle. Developers and agents query the graph in dev to understand blast radius before code is written. CI pipelines query it to validate changes before merge. Staging queries it to catch drift between IaC and actual state. By the time a change reaches production, it's already been validated at every step. One graph, every agent.

SkaLogs can also fit with your existing ELK instances, and can provide a complete toolbox to make your Log ingestion and transformation easier with a 100% Log dedicated ETL with multiple guided workflows.

SkaLogs is an IT Monitoring solution (ITOA/AIOps), a Security Information and Event Management Solution (SIEM), and a Business Activity Monitoring Solution (BAM).

Any Cloud. One Platform. Cloud Made Easy.

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B sales benchmark.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company — the company a sales operator is targeting.
  • A CANDIDATE company — a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide whether the CANDIDATE is a plausible lookalike of the SEED for
B2B sales prospecting. A plausible lookalike is a company a sales rep
working the SEED account would also want to work — same kind of
business model, overlapping product category, or buyer persona.

Rules:
  - relevant = true only when the candidate is clearly the same kind of
    company (same model + overlapping customer or buyer persona).
  - Require both: (1) the candidate's primary product/service overlaps a core
    offering of the seed, and (2) the same buyer or user would reasonably
    evaluate both for the same job to be done. A shared generic taxonomy label
    or keyword is not enough.
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. Those are not benchmark
    constraints: a smaller or larger company can be a relevant lookalike.
    Ignore any such metadata in the candidate record when deciding relevance.
  - relevant = false for unrelated industries, parent companies,
    customers/clients of the seed, agencies/consultancies that serve the
    category (rather than competing), and parody/duplicate entries.
  - When in doubt, label false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words.

Examples:
  - HubSpot ↔ a smaller CRM/marketing-automation platform: true.
  - HubSpot ↔ a lead-generation agency using HubSpot for clients: false.
  - Shopify ↔ an online-store/e-commerce platform: true.
  - Shopify ↔ a payment processor with no storefront platform: false.
  - Grab ↔ a ride-hailing marketplace: true.
  - Grab ↔ a traditional car-rental operator with no on-demand marketplace: false.
  - Rippling ↔ a smaller HRIS/payroll platform: true.
  - Rippling ↔ device-security software for mobile workers: false.
  - Brex ↔ a corporate-card and spend-management platform: true.
  - Brex ↔ consumer personal-finance budgeting software: false.
  - OpenAI ↔ a foundation-model/API company: true.
  - OpenAI ↔ a consultancy that implements AI tools for clients: false.
  - Datadog ↔ an application-performance-monitoring and observability platform: true.
  - Datadog ↔ a generic IT consulting firm: false.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ an endpoint-security platform: true.
  - CrowdStrike ↔ a general-purpose IT monitoring tool with no security product: false.
  - Procore ↔ construction project-management software: true.
  - Procore ↔ a construction contractor: false.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ field-service management software for trades businesses: true.
  - ServiceTitan ↔ a plumbing company that uses field-service software: false.
  - Teladoc ↔ a virtual-care/telehealth platform: true.
  - Teladoc ↔ a health-insurance carrier with no telehealth product: false.
  - Veeva ↔ life-sciences CRM or clinical-operations software: true.
  - Veeva ↔ a generic CRM with no life-sciences focus: false.

## About

GreptimeDB is the open-source Observability 2.0 database — treating

properties.name: Greptime | The Single Database for Observability on S3
properties.description:
GreptimeDB is the open-source Observability 2.0 database — treating metrics, logs, and traces as unified wide events instead of three separate pillars.

The three-pillar model (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger) creates data silos, redundant infrastructure, and cross-system correlation pain. GreptimeDB replaces all three with one columnar engine on object storage, enabling cross-signal SQL JOINs, up to 50x cost reduction, and native support for emerging workloads like AI agent observability.

Why teams switch:
▪️Logs: Full-text indexing where Loki only indexes labels. 10x faster queries, 30% lower TCO. (OB Cloud: billions of logs daily across 170+ availability zones.)
▪️Metrics: Compute-storage separation — no more Thanos/Mimir complexity. SQL + PromQL replaces Prometheus + your data warehouse.
▪️Traces: Columnar storage vs. ES inverted indexes — 45x less storage, Jaeger-compatible, one-week migration.
▪️AI/LLM: Store high-volume conversation data, agent traces, and token metrics via OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions.

Written in Rust, OpenTelemetry-native, deploys on Kubernetes with compute-storage separation. Used in production by teams processing billions of data points daily.

▪️Open-source: https://github.com/GreptimeTeam/greptimedb
▪️Learn more in Why GreptimeDB: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/why-greptimedb/
▪️Learn about Observability 2.0: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/observability-2/
▪️Enterprise & Cloud: https://greptime.com

# Manifest

Manifest is a Technology, Information and Internet company. ManifestIT is a change observability platform that helps intelligently evaluate risk, quantify impact, and break down silos between tools and teams. Manifest employs 24 people. Headquartered in Menlo Park, California, United States. Its workforce is distributed across India, United States, and Canada.

## About

Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has l

properties.name: Manifest
properties.description:
Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has lived in the heads of senior engineers, architects, and platform teams. A developer who needs it pings someone, digs through Slack, or learns it the hard way after an outage. That works, slowly. Agents don't have that option at all. Connection pool limits, IAM scopes, mesh policies, secret bindings, downstream consumers, live drift—none of it is in the code, and none of it is in any place an agent can reach.

We've built Manifest to compile that context into software. We continuously assemble a deterministic, time-versioned graph of the customer's full application stack: code, IaC, cloud, Kubernetes, IAM, secrets, mesh, CI/CD, on-prem. The architectural commitment is retrieval separated from reasoning. The graph is built once, continuously, and queryable as data, so the agents reasoning on top don't each have to investigate the environment from scratch. The graph is the context layer that developers and coding agents query before they make a change, so the code (whether written by a human or an agent) fits the system it's about to touch. Because the graph captures every change attributed to actor and timestamp, configuration drift and unauthorized changes surface the moment they happen instead of being discovered weeks later in an outage or audit.

Manifest works from the earliest moments of the lifecycle. Developers and agents query the graph in dev to understand blast radius before code is written. CI pipelines query it to validate changes before merge. Staging queries it to catch drift between IaC and actual state. By the time a change reaches production, it's already been validated at every step. One graph, every agent.

CubeAPM is a managed, self-hosted observability platform that bridges the gap between cloud-based monitoring tools and traditional on-prem setups. Built for modern DevOps, SRE, and engineering teams, CubeAPM provides a full-stack observability suite - APM, Log Management, Infrastructure Monitoring, Real-User Monitoring, Synthetic Monitoring, and Error Tracking - all deployed inside your VPC or on-premises.

Running in your VPC/on-prem ensures complete data residency compliance, low latency and cost efficiency, while it’s managed like SaaS - the upgrades, tuning, and maintenance are handled by CubeAPM, not your team. It is OpenTelemetry-native but also provides multi-agent support and seamlessly integrates with agents of New Relic, Datadog, Prometheus, Elastic & Open Telemetry. Hence the switch from your current tool to CubeAPM can be done within minutes.

The platform uses AI-driven smart sampling to store only meaningful data, reducing storage needs by up to 95% and making costs predictable. Users benefit from unlimited retention, low-latency dashboards, and enterprise-grade support with response times measured in minutes.

Leading enterprises like Policybazaar ($10B market cap), Delhivery ($4.5B market cap), Practo, Redbus, and Mamaearth who ingest petabytes of data monthly, have transitioned from traditional observability setups to CubeAPM for faster MTTR and predictable pricing.

entity.name: Greptime | The Single Database for Observability on S3
entity.description:
GreptimeDB is the open-source Observability 2.0 database — treating metrics, logs, and traces as unified wide events instead of three separate pillars.

The three-pillar model (Prometheus + Loki + Jaeger) creates data silos, redundant infrastructure, and cross-system correlation pain. GreptimeDB replaces all three with one columnar engine on object storage, enabling cross-signal SQL JOINs, up to 50x cost reduction, and native support for emerging workloads like AI agent observability.

Why teams switch:
▪️Logs: Full-text indexing where Loki only indexes labels. 10x faster queries, 30% lower TCO. (OB Cloud: billions of logs daily across 170+ availability zones.)
▪️Metrics: Compute-storage separation — no more Thanos/Mimir complexity. SQL + PromQL replaces Prometheus + your data warehouse.
▪️Traces: Columnar storage vs. ES inverted indexes — 45x less storage, Jaeger-compatible, one-week migration.
▪️AI/LLM: Store high-volume conversation data, agent traces, and token metrics via OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions.

Written in Rust, OpenTelemetry-native, deploys on Kubernetes with compute-storage separation. Used in production by teams processing billions of data points daily.

▪️Open-source: https://github.com/GreptimeTeam/greptimedb
▪️Learn more in Why GreptimeDB: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/why-greptimedb/
▪️Learn about Observability 2.0: https://docs.greptime.com/user-guide/concepts/observability-2/
▪️Enterprise & Cloud: https://greptime.com

entity.name: Manifest
entity.description:
Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has lived in the heads of senior engineers, architects, and platform teams. A developer who needs it pings someone, digs through Slack, or learns it the hard way after an outage. That works, slowly. Agents don't have that option at all. Connection pool limits, IAM scopes, mesh policies, secret bindings, downstream consumers, live drift—none of it is in the code, and none of it is in any place an agent can reach.

We've built Manifest to compile that context into software. We continuously assemble a deterministic, time-versioned graph of the customer's full application stack: code, IaC, cloud, Kubernetes, IAM, secrets, mesh, CI/CD, on-prem. The architectural commitment is retrieval separated from reasoning. The graph is built once, continuously, and queryable as data, so the agents reasoning on top don't each have to investigate the environment from scratch. The graph is the context layer that developers and coding agents query before they make a change, so the code (whether written by a human or an agent) fits the system it's about to touch. Because the graph captures every change attributed to actor and timestamp, configuration drift and unauthorized changes surface the moment they happen instead of being discovered weeks later in an outage or audit.

Manifest works from the earliest moments of the lifecycle. Developers and agents query the graph in dev to understand blast radius before code is written. CI pipelines query it to validate changes before merge. Staging queries it to catch drift between IaC and actual state. By the time a change reaches production, it's already been validated at every step. One graph, every agent.

You are an evaluator scoring company lookalike results for a B2B sales benchmark.

You will be given:
  • A SEED company — the company a sales operator is targeting.
  • A CANDIDATE company — a lookalike returned by a vendor's API.

Decide whether the CANDIDATE is a plausible lookalike of the SEED for
B2B sales prospecting. A plausible lookalike is a company a sales rep
working the SEED account would also want to work — same kind of
business model, overlapping product category, or buyer persona.

Rules:
  - relevant = true only when the candidate is clearly the same kind of
    company (same model + overlapping customer or buyer persona).
  - Require both: (1) the candidate's primary product/service overlaps a core
    offering of the seed, and (2) the same buyer or user would reasonably
    evaluate both for the same job to be done. A shared generic taxonomy label
    or keyword is not enough.
  - Do NOT require comparable company size, headcount, revenue, funding,
    geography, maturity, or platform breadth. Those are not benchmark
    constraints: a smaller or larger company can be a relevant lookalike.
    Ignore any such metadata in the candidate record when deciding relevance.
  - relevant = false for unrelated industries, parent companies,
    customers/clients of the seed, agencies/consultancies that serve the
    category (rather than competing), and parody/duplicate entries.
  - When in doubt, label false.
  - Keep the rationale ≤ 25 words.

  extras: {"url": "https://manifestit.ai/", "entity": {"name": "Manifest", "foundedYear": null, "description": "Coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, and Copilot have shown how much developer velocity AI can unlock, but the code they write only works if it fits the environment it deploys into. Until now, this context has lived in the heads of senior engineers, architects, and platform teams. A developer who needs it pings someone, digs through Slack, or learns it the hard way after an outage. That works, slowly. Agents don't have that option at all. Connection pool limits, IAM scopes, mesh policies, secret bindings, downstream consumers, live drift—none of it is in the code, and none of it is in any place an agent can reach.\n\nWe've built Manifest to compile that context into software. We continuously assemble a deterministic, time-versioned graph of the customer's full application stack: code, IaC, cloud, Kubernetes, IAM, secrets, mesh, CI/CD, on-prem. The architectural commitment is retrieval separated from reasoning. The graph is built once, continuously, and queryable as data, so the agents reasoning on top don't each have to investigate the environment from scratch. The graph is the context layer that developers and coding agents query before they make a change, so the code (whether written by a human or an agent) fits the system it's about to touch.
